article.title: Replace Mitch McConnell
article.author: Berry Craig
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Charles Booker lost bids for the U.S. Senate in 2020 and 2022. “I didn't think I would ever run again,” Kentucky's Democratic Senate hopeful told about 100 supporters who gathered in front of Paducah’s historic old Hotel Metropolitan. “This is Rocky 3 for me.” The crowd laughed, cheered and waved Booker-for-Senate 2026 signs appreciatively. A 42-year-old former state lawmaker from Louisville, his hometown, Booker is the first African American to win a major party nomination for the Senate in Kentucky. In previous campaigns, he had stopped at the hotel, now a museum, which dated to Jim Crow times when segregation and race discrimination were the law and the social order in the South and in border states like Kentucky. The color bar was rigid in Paducah, in far western Kentucky where the Tennessee and Ohio rivers converge. Blacks couldn’t stay in white hotels. “This hotel and the nearby Purple Room were popular stops for leading African American performers and musicians touring the South during the mid-20th cen, on what was called the ‘Chitlin Circuit,'" says a state historical marker. “Other notable guests included civil rights leaders, the Harlem Globetrotters, & Negro League Baseball players.” Also, according to the marker, the hotel was added to the National Register in 2002. Related: Hegseth’s Holy War on Fat Generals Meets the Weight of History Before Booker took the microphone on the hotel’s broad front porch, Drew Williams, the First District Democratic candidate for congress, and local candidates took turns speaking briefly. Booker said his campaign shows “what humanity looks like-regular people from Pikeville to the Purchase, the hood to the holler, all of us.” He wrote a book titled From the Hood to the Holler: A Story of Separate Worlds, Shared Dreams, and the Fight for America's Future. Booker said his aim is “shining a light for justice, shining a light for freedom…for love” and against “all this hate and gross bigotry.” He said he believes “that politics can be different-that we can have a government that reflects us, that represents us and is accountable to us.” In 2018, Booker was elected to the state House of Representatives from District 43 in Louisville, the state's largest city. He had one of the safest Democratic seats in the legislature. But after a single term, he set his sights on the Senate. He recalled that when he “stepped out on faith” to make his first Senate run, “people said, ‘Are you crazy Charles?’” He said he replied, “No, this is what I've got to do. We can bring people together…We lit a spark.” Related: JD Vance, Abdul El-Sayed and the GOP’s Search for a Racist Sweet Spot Booker’s Republican opponent, hard right Sixth District Congressman Andy Barr, is heavily favored to win, according to pundits and independent national polls. Barr, a Trump loyalist, opted against another House term to go after the retiring Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell’s seat. Booker said when people ask him if he has a shot to win, he replies, “We already won, and you know who knows it? The president of the United States who came to Kentucky because this race is tight.” Trump traveled to Highland Heights in northern Kentucky on Oct. 17 to plug Barr and ultra-conservative Republican Ed Gallrein, who, with the president’s blessing, defeated incumbent Thomas Massie, a sometimes sharp Trump critic, in the May GOP primary. “Everybody is fed up with the status quo,” Booker said, calling out “politicians who would rather put a data center in your backyard,” who refuse to “listen to you and refuse to “drive down the cost of living. Politicians who would rather cut Medicaid so that Elon Musk can get a tax break. Politicians who would give a blank check to endless war instead of taking care of teachers and making sure children have food to eat.” Booker said in his third try for the Senate, he senses “something different is happening. I see it all across Kentucky, everywhere I go.” Related: They Don’t Call James Carville the “Ragin’ Cajun” for Nothing But he warned, “If we don't take a stand now, we will not have an opportunity for the future. These rising prices [will]… get worse if we don't take this stand.” He said even Trump voters are rallying to him in addition to “people who never voted before.” Booker said because “we don't have the national support,” victory will be “even sweeter” because "victory will be ours.” He wrapped up by urging his fans to “spread the good news…. Tell the people you love, tell those you like and tell some folks you don’t like that much.” He added, “and even if your loved one, your colleague, your friend who has never voted for,” he smiled and hesitated for effect, “…someone who’s as handsome as me. Tell them to take a chance anyway.” The crowd got the last quip and burst into more laughter, cheering and applause. He predicted that “in a few days, we're going to be celebrating a victory, not just a victory of winning the Senate race. But the victory of continuing our pursuit that Dr. King spoke of when he said, ‘The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.' This is how that arc ends. This is how we do the arc.” He concluded by musing. “How poetic will it be to replace Mitch McConnell-to replace a man who was elected when I was two weeks old. How poetic would it be in a time of so much chaos, in a time of so much corruption…that we stood up. That we took our power back. That we said enough is enough. So, let's do it.”
